claim: Glutamatergic neurons in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) function as respiratory chemoreceptors by regulating breathing in response to tissue CO2/H+.
source: Glutamatergic neurons in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) function as respiratory chemoreceptors by regulating breathing in response to tissue CO2/H+.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about RTN neurons, presented as background in the abstract.

claim: Loss of inhibitory neural activity in a mouse model of Dravet syndrome disinhibited RTN chemoreceptors and destabilized breathing.
source: In the context of disease, we showed that loss of inhibitory neural activity in a mouse model of Dravet syndrome disinhibited RTN chemoreceptors and destabilized breathing (Kuo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Kuo et al., 2019).

claim: The parafacial region contains a limited diversity of inhibitory neurons including somatostatin (Sst)-, parvalbumin (Pvalb)-, and cholecystokinin (Cck)-expressing neurons.
source: Here, we show the parafacial region contains a limited diversity of inhibitory neurons including somatostatin (Sst)-, parvalbumin (Pvalb)-, and cholecystokinin (Cck)-expressing neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1C).

claim: Sst-expressing interneurons appear uniquely inhibited by CO2/H+.
source: Of these, Sst-expressing interneurons appear uniquely inhibited by CO2/H+.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing CO2/H+ sensitivity of Sst+ neurons (Figure 2).

claim: RTN chemoreceptors receive inhibitory input that is withdrawn in a CO2/H+-dependent manner.
source: We also show RTN chemoreceptors receive inhibitory input that is withdrawn in a CO2/H+-dependent manner
evidence: This claim is supported by synaptic current recordings showing CO2/H+-dependent changes in sIPSC frequency (Figure 3).

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of Sst+ parafacial neurons increases baseline breathing.
source: chemogenetic suppression of Sst+ parafacial neurons, but not Pvalb+ or Cck+ neurons, increases baseline breathing.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo plethysmography experiments using DREADD-mediated inhibition (Figure 5).

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of Pvalb+ parafacial neurons does not increase baseline breathing.
source: chemogenetic suppression of Sst+ parafacial neurons, but not Pvalb+ or Cck+ neurons, increases baseline breathing.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo plethysmography experiments (Figure 5B).

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of Cck+ parafacial neurons does not increase baseline breathing.
source: chemogenetic suppression of Sst+ parafacial neurons, but not Pvalb+ or Cck+ neurons, increases baseline breathing.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo plethysmography experiments (Figure 5C).

claim: Sst-expressing parafacial neurons contribute to RTN chemoreception and respiratory activity.
source: These results suggest Sst-expressing parafacial neurons contribute to RTN chemoreception and respiratory activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined cellular, synaptic, and behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chemosensitive RTN neurons express the transcription factor Phox2b.
source: Chemosensitive RTN neurons express the transcription factor Phox2b (Stornetta et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Chemosensitive RTN neurons are glutamatergic.
source: are glutamatergic (Mulkey et al., 2004; Weston et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RTN neurons are intrinsically responsive to CO2/H+ by mechanisms involving acid inhibition of TWIK-related Acid-Sensitive K+ channel 2 (TASK-2).
source: are intrinsically responsive to CO2/H+ by mechanisms involving acid inhibition of TWIK-related Acid-Sensitive K+ channel 2 (TASK-2; Wang et al., 2013a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: RTN neurons are intrinsically responsive to CO2/H+ by mechanisms involving activation of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPR4).
source: and activation of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPR4; Kumar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Activity of RTN chemoreceptors is subject to modulation by purinergic signaling.
source: Activity of RTN chemoreceptors is also subject to modulation by purinergic signaling (Mulkey et al., 2006; Wenker et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Purinergic signaling modulating RTN chemoreceptors most likely comes from local astrocytes.
source: most likely from local astrocytes (Gourine et al., 2010; Huckstepp et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Activity of RTN chemoreceptors is subject to modulation by excitatory synaptic input.
source: as well as excitatory (Lazarenko et al., 2011; Mulkey et al., 2007) and inhibitory (Guyenet et al., 2005; Moreira et al., 2007; Takakura et al., 2007) synaptic input.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Activity of RTN chemoreceptors is subject to modulation by inhibitory synaptic input.
source: as well as excitatory (Lazarenko et al., 2011; Mulkey et al., 2007) and inhibitory (Guyenet et al., 2005; Moreira et al., 2007; Takakura et al., 2007) synaptic input.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RTN chemoreceptors have numerous presumptive inhibitory (symmetric) and glutamatergic synapses (asymmetric).
source: In addition, previous work showed using a Phox2b-eGFP reporter line that RTN chemoreceptors have numerous presumptive inhibitory (symmetric) and glutamatergic synapses (asymmetric) (Lazarenko et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Unilateral RTN injection of glutamate receptor blockers (AP5 or CNQX) decreased baseline breathing in urethane-anesthetized rats.
source: These results are supported by functional evidence showing in urethane-anesthetized rats that unilateral RTN injection of glutamate receptor blockers (AP5 or CNQX) decreased baseline breathing and the ventilatory response to CO2 (Nattie and Li, 1995)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Unilateral RTN injection of glutamate receptor blockers decreased the ventilatory response to CO2 in urethane-anesthetized rats.
source: These results are supported by functional evidence showing in urethane-anesthetized rats that unilateral RTN injection of glutamate receptor blockers (AP5 or CNQX) decreased baseline breathing and the ventilatory response to CO2 (Nattie and Li, 1995)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Unilateral RTN injection of the GABAA receptor blocker bicuculline stimulated baseline breathing in urethane-anesthetized rats.
source: whereas unilateral RTN injection of the GABAA receptor blocker bicuculline stimulated baseline breathing and blunted CO2-stimulated respiratory activity (Nattie et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Unilateral RTN injection of bicuculline blunted CO2-stimulated respiratory activity in urethane-anesthetized rats.
source: whereas unilateral RTN injection of the GABAA receptor blocker bicuculline stimulated baseline breathing and blunted CO2-stimulated respiratory activity (Nattie et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic drive to the RTN from distal and possibly local sources are required for maintenance of baseline breathing and CO2/H+ chemoreception.
source: This suggests glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic drive to the RTN from distal and possibly local sources are required for maintenance of baseline breathing and CO2/H+ chemoreception.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited pharmacological studies.

claim: The RTN contains CO2/H+-activated and -inhibited neurons that communicate through CO2/H+-dependent excitatory and inhibitory interactions.
source: Based on in vivo multi-electrode array recordings in cats that showed the RTN contains CO2/H+-activated and -inhibited neurons that communicate through CO2/H+-dependent excitatory and inhibitory interactions (Ott et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Single cells from the ventral parafacial region were isolated from 10-day-old wild type C57BL/6J mice (N = 16; 8 of each sex).
source: Single cells from the ventral parafacial region were isolated from 10-day-old wild type C57BL/6J (N = 16; 8 of each sex).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used for single-cell RNA sequencing.

claim: Tamoxifen treatment did not affect the proportion of cells obtained or relative transcript profiles across all major cell types.
source: However, since tamoxifen treatment did not affect the proportion of cells obtained or relative transcript profiles across all major cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), these data sets were pooled.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: After quality control filtering and doublet removal, 11,810 cells were analyzed with a median of 2892 unique transcripts (UMIs) and 1472 genes per cell.
source: After quality control filtering and doublet removal (see Materials and methods), we analyzed 11,810 cells with a median of 2892 unique transcripts (UMIs) and 1472 genes per cell.
evidence: This describes the results of the scRNA-seq data processing.

claim: Non-neuronal cells comprised roughly 90% of the dataset.
source: Non-neuronal cells comprised roughly 90% of the dataset
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: The neuronal population included 197 vesicular glutamate-transport type 2 (Vglut2+; Slc17a6) glutamatergic excitatory neurons.
source: A second mixture model was then used to classify the neurons into three groups: vesicular glutamate-transport type 2 (Vglut2+; Slc17a6) glutamatergic excitatory neurons (N = 197)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: The neuronal population included 445 vesicular GABA transporter (Vgat+; Slc32a1) inhibitory neurons.
source: vesicular GABA transporter (Vgat+; Slc32a1) inhibitory neurons (N = 445)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: The resulting neuronal populations had a median of 4587 UMIs and 2317 genes per Slc17a6+ neuron.
source: The resulting neuronal populations had markedly higher molecular content, with a median of 4587 UMIs and 2317 genes per Slc17a6+ neuron
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: The resulting neuronal populations had a median of 4439 UMIs and 2299 genes per Slc32a1+ neuron.
source: and 4439 UMIs and 2299 genes per Slc32a1+ neuron.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: The population of Slc17a6+ cells includes two clusters (Slc17a6 clusters 1–2) of Phox2b-positive and Nmb expressing neurons with similar levels of Gpr4 and Kcnk5 but differ in galanin (Gal) expression.
source: The population of Slc17a6+ cells does not overlap with Chat+ cells and includes two clusters (Slc17a6 clusters 1–2) of Phox2b-positive and Nmb expressing neurons with similar levels of Gpr4 (G-protein-coupled receptor 4) and Kcnk5 (TASK-2; K2P5) but differ in galanin (Gal) expression (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The molecular profiles of Slc17a6 clusters 1-2 are largely consistent with that of RTN chemoreceptors.
source: The molecular profiles of these clusters are largely consistent with that of RTN chemoreceptors (Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim compares current findings to prior work cited.

claim: Sympathetic C1 catecholamine neurons (Slc17a6 cluster 4) are identified by expression of tyrosine hydroxylase (Th) and Phox2b and the absence of Nmb.
source: Sympathetic C1 catecholamine neurons (Slc17a6 cluster 4) are identified by expression of tyrosine hydroxylase (Th) and Phox2b and the absence of Nmb (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and citation to prior work.

claim: All four glutamatergic clusters had detectable levels of stathmin 4 (Stmn4), suggesting these populations are not yet fully differentiated.
source: All four glutamatergic clusters had detectable levels of stathmin 4 (Stmn4, encodes a microtubual binding protein [Holmfeldt et al., 2003]), suggesting these populations are not yet fully differentiated.
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns and citation to prior work about Stmn4 function.

claim: The population of parafacial inhibitory Slc32a1+ neurons was composed of 7 discrete clusters.
source: The population of parafacial inhibitory Slc32a1+ neurons was composed of 7 discrete clusters that could be distinguished by largely non-overlapping expression of somatostatin (Sst, Slc32a1 clusters 3, 6–7), parvalbumin (Pvalb, Slc32a1 cluster 5), cholecystokinin (Cck, Slc32a1 cluster 1) and the more recently identified interneuron marker (Abs et al., 2018) neuron-derived neurotrophic factor (Ndnf, Slc32a1 cluster 2) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Sst+ interneurons were the most abundant inhibitory cell type in the parafacial region.
source: Of these, Sst+ interneurons were the most abundant cell type
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the scRNA-seq data.

claim: Sst+ interneurons varied in expression of calretinin (Calb2, Slc32a1 cluster 3), reelin (Reln, Slc32a1 cluster 6) and neuronal nitric oxide synthase 1 (Nos1, Slc32a1 clusters 3, 7).
source: but varied in expression of calretinin (Calb2, Slc32a1 cluster 3), reelin (Reln, Slc32a1 cluster 6) and neuronal nitric oxide synthase 1 (Nos1, Slc32a1 clusters 3, 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: All Slc32a1+ parafacial neurons express lysosome-associated membrane protein 5 (Lamp5).
source: Consistent with other brainstem regions, we found that all Slc32a1+ parafacial neurons also express lysosome-associated membrane protein 5 (Lamp5) (Koebis et al., 2019) (not shown)
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and citation to prior work.

claim: Most Slc32a1+ parafacial neurons express the sodium- and chloride-dependent glycine transporter 2 (GlyT2; Slc6a5).
source: and most express the sodium- and chloride-dependent glycine transporter 2 (GlyT2; Slc6a5) (Hirrlinger et al., 2019; Figure 1C), suggesting they have the capacity to release GABA and glycine.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and citation to prior work.

claim: Slc32a1+ parafacial neurons have the capacity to release GABA and glycine.
source: suggesting they have the capacity to release GABA and glycine.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of GlyT2 and Slc32a1.

claim: The ventral parafacial region was devoid of interneurons that express the serotonin receptor 5HT3aR (Htr3a), vasoactive intestinal peptide (Vip), or neuropeptide Y (Npy).
source: However, in contrast to the cortex (Lee et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2018), the ventral parafacial region was devoid of interneurons that express the serotonin receptor 5HT3aR (Htr3a), vasoactive intestinal peptide (Vip), or neuropeptide Y (Npy) (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and contrasted with cited prior work in cortex.

claim: TdT labeled Slc32a1 cells are distributed throughout the ventral parafacial region including juxtaposed to Phox2b-immunoreactive RTN chemoreceptors.
source: We confirmed that TdT labeled Slc32a1 cells are distributed throughout the ventral parafacial region including juxtaposed to Phox2b-immunoreactive RTN chemoreceptors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: ~85% of Slc32a1+ cells co-express glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD67; Gad1) and GlyT2 (Slc6a5).
source: In-line with our scRNA-seq results, we found by fluorescent in situ hybridization that ~85% of Slc32a1+ cells (n = 57 cells) co-express glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD67; Gad1) and GlyT2 (Slc6a5) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Scn1a is expressed by all parafacial neurons, particularly inhibitory neurons that showed relatively higher levels of expression compared to glutamatergic neurons.
source: Also, consistent with our previous work showing that expression of a Dravet syndrome-associated Scn1a mutation disrupted RTN chemoreception and respiratory activity (Kuo et al., 2016), we found that Scn1a is expressed by all parafacial neurons, particularly inhibitory neurons that showed relatively higher levels of expression compared to glutamatergic neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and citation to prior work.

claim: Exposure to 10% CO2 decreased activity in 48 of 130 (37%) fluorescent parafacial neurons by an average of 2.0 ± 0.2 Hz.
source: By this criterion, we found that exposure to 10% CO2 decreased activity in 48 of 130 (37%) fluorescent parafacial neurons by an average of 2.0 ± 0.2 Hz (Figure 2Ai,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2.

claim: The majority of parafacial inhibitory neurons (56%) did not respond to 10% CO2 stimulus.
source: The majority of parafacial inhibitory neurons (56%) did not respond to stimulus and so were considered CO2/H+-insensitive (Figure 2Bi,D)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2.

claim: A small subset of fluorescent parafacial neurons (7%) showed an excitatory response to CO2.
source: while a small subset of fluorescent parafacial neurons (7%) showed an excitatory response to CO2 (F2,130 = 91.23, p<0.001) (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The inhibitory effect of CO2/H+ on chemosensitive RTN neurons was retained when purinergic signaling was blocked by bath application of PPADS (100 µM) and 8-PT (10 µM).
source: We also found the inhibitory effect of CO2/H+ on chemosensitive RTN neurons was retained when purinergic signaling was blocked by bath application of pyridoxalphosphate-6-azophenyl-2',4'-disulfonic acid (PPADS; 100 µM) and 8-phenyltheophylline (8-PT; 10 µM) (T7 = 0.1515, p>0.05)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings with pharmacological blockers shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The inhibitory effect of CO2/H+ on chemosensitive RTN neurons was retained in the presence of ionotropic receptor blockers including CNQX (10 μM), gabazine (10 μM), and strychnine (2 μM).
source: or in the presence of ionotropic receptor blockers including CNQX (10 μM) to block AMPA/kainite receptors, gabazine (10 μM) to block GABAA receptors, and strychnine (2 μM) to block glycine receptors (T7 = 3.100, p=0.02) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings with pharmacological blockers shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Parafacial inhibitory neurons are intrinsically CO2/H+-sensitive.
source: These results suggest parafacial inhibitory neurons are intrinsically CO2/H+-sensitive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of CO2/H+ responses in the presence of synaptic and purinergic blockers.

claim: 5 of 5 CO2/H+-inhibited parafacial neurons were Sst-immunoreactive.
source: We found that 5 of 5 CO2/H+-inhibited cells were Sst-immunoreactive (Figure 2Aii)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2Aii.

claim: 0 of 5 CO2/H+-insensitive parafacial neurons expressed Sst.
source: whereas 0 of 5 CO2/H+-insensitive cells expressed Sst (Figure 2Bii).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2Bii.

claim: CO2/H+-inhibited parafacial neurons are one or more types (clusters 3, 6–7) of Sst-expressing inhibitory neurons.
source: These results suggest CO2/H+-inhibited parafacial neurons are one or more types (clusters 3, 6–7; Figure 1C) of Sst-expressing inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on immunohistochemistry and scRNA-seq data.

claim: RTN neurons were considered chemosensitive if they show some level of spontaneous activity under control conditions and a robust firing rate response to 10% CO2 (Δ1.6 ± 0.36 Hz; N = 7 cells).
source: As previously defined (Kuo et al., 2016), RTN neurons were considered chemosensitive if they show some level of spontaneous activity under control conditions and a robust firing rate response to 10% CO2 (Δ1.6 ± 0.36 Hz; N = 7 cells).
evidence: This describes the criteria used to identify chemosensitive RTN neurons, based on prior work and current data.

claim: Under control conditions (5% CO2), chemosensitive RTN neurons showed sIPSCs with an average frequency of 0.22 Hz and amplitude of 13.7 pA.
source: Under control conditions (5% CO2), chemosensitive RTN neurons showed sIPSCs with an average frequency of 0.22 Hz and amplitude of 13.7 pA (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3.

claim: The kinetics of sIPSCs recorded in RTN neurons are similar to what has been described in other brain regions; average rise (10%–90%) and decay (90%–10%) times of 3.1 ms and 25.5 ms, respectively.
source: The kinetics of sIPSCs recorded in RTN neurons are similar to what has been described in other brain regions (Ali et al., 2007; Banks and Pearce, 2000); average rise (10%–90%) and decay (90%–10%) times of 3.1 ms and 25.5 ms, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data and comparison to cited prior work.

claim: Exposure to 10% CO2 decreases sIPSC frequency in RTN neurons to 0.1 ± 0.06 Hz (F2,6=21.04; p<0.001; N = 7 cells total).
source: Exposure to 10% CO2 decreases sIPSC frequency to 0.1 ± 0.06 Hz (F2,6=21.04; p<0.001; N = 7 cells total) (Figure 3A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Exposure to 10% CO2 decreased sIPSC amplitude in RTN neurons (F2,6=6.58; p<0.05).
source: and decreased sIPSC amplitude (F2,6=6.58; p<0.05) (Figure 3C)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Exposure to 10% CO2 had no change in sIPSC rise (3.7 ms; p=0.516) or decay (27.7 ms; p=0.268) times in RTN neurons.
source: but with no change in sIPSC rise (3.7 msl p=0.516) or decay (27.7 ms; p=0.268) times.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: Bath application of bicuculline (10 µM) and strychnine (2 µM) eliminated all sIPSCs in RTN neurons, confirming they are mediated by GABA or glycinergic input.
source: Subsequent bath application of bicuculline (10 µM) to block GABAA receptors and strychnine (2 µM) to block glycine receptors eliminated all sIPSCs, thus confirming they are mediated by GABA or glycinergic input (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A subset of parafacial Slc32a1 neurons are inhibited by CO2/H+ and contribute to RTN chemoreception by a mechanism involving disinhibition.
source: these results are consistent with the possibility that a subset of parafacial Slc32a1 neurons are inhibited by CO2/H+ and contribute to RTN chemoreception by a mechanism involving disinhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the synaptic recording data showing CO2/H+-dependent withdrawal of inhibitory input.

claim: Bath application of bicuculine (10 µM) and strychnine (2 µM) increased baseline activity of RTN chemoreceptors by 0.7 ± 0.2 Hz (T12 = 2.201, p=0.022).
source: In cell-attached voltage-clamp mode, bath application of bicuculine (10 µM) and strychnine (2 µM) increased baseline activity of RTN chemoreceptors by 0.7 ± 0.2 Hz (T12 = 2.201, p=0.022) (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: Inhibitory input partly limits activity of RTN chemoreceptors under baseline conditions.
source: This finding suggests inhibitory input partly limits activity of RTN chemoreceptors under baseline conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of GABA/glycine receptor blockers on baseline activity.

claim: The firing response of RTN chemoreceptors to 10% CO2 was similar under control conditions and in the presence of bicuculine and strychnine (Δ −0.3 ± 0.2 Hz; T12 = 1.246, p>0.05).
source: We also found the firing response to 10% CO2 was similar under control conditions and in the presence of bicuculine and strychnine (Δ −0.3 ± 0.2 Hz; T12 = 1.246, p>0.05) (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: CO2/H+-dependent inhibitory transmission regulates activity of RTN chemoreceptors under baseline conditions but not during exposure to high CO2.
source: These results suggest CO2/H+-dependent inhibitory transmission regulates activity of RTN chemoreceptors under baseline conditions but not during exposure to high CO2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of GABA/glycine receptor blockers under baseline vs. high CO2 conditions.

claim: Under control conditions (5% CO2) and at a holding potential of −60 mV, chemosensitive RTN neurons exhibit sEPSCs with an average frequency of 0.33 Hz and amplitude of −12.6 pA.
source: Under control conditions (5% CO2) and at a holding potential of −60 mV chemosensitive RTN neurons exhibit sEPSCs with an average frequency of 0.33 Hz and amplitude of −12.6 pA (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: The kinetics of RTN sEPSCs are similar to AMPA-mediated events described in other brain regions; average rise (10%–90%) and decay (90%–10%) times of 1.2 ms and 4.9 ms, respectively.
source: The kinetics of RTN sEPSCs are similar to AMPA-mediated events described in other brain regions (Magee and Cook, 2000; Rodriguez-Molina et al., 2007; Selyanko et al., 1979); average rise (10%–90%) and decay (90%–10%) times of 1.2 ms and 4.9 ms, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data and comparison to cited prior work.

claim: Exposure to 10% CO2 increased sEPSC frequency in RTN neurons to 0.65 ± 0.08 Hz (F2,7 = 26.91; p<0.001).
source: Exposure to 10% CO2 increased sEPSC frequency to 0.65 ± 0.08 Hz (F2,7 = 26.91; p<0.001) (Figure 4A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Exposure to 10% CO2 had no change in sEPSC amplitude (F2,7 = 1.398; p>0.05) in RTN neurons.
source: but with no change in sEPSC amplitude (F2,7 = 1.398; p>0.05) (Figure 4C)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Exposure to 10% CO2 had no change in sEPSC kinetics (rise time 1.3 ms, p=0.5772; decay time 5.0 ms, p=0.9642) in RTN neurons.
source: or kinetics (rise time 1.3 ms, p=0.5772; decay time 5.0 ms, p=0.9642).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: CO2/H+ increases the sEPSC/sIPSC ratio in RTN neurons from 1.5 to 8.9 (T5 = 3.70; p<0.05).
source: Furthermore, when both excitatory and inhibitory spontaneous synaptic events were characterized in the same cells (N = 6), we confirmed that CO2/H+ increases the sEPSC/sIPSC ratio from 1.5 to 8.9 (Figure 4F) (T5 = 3.70; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The RTN functions as a CO2/H+-sensing network where excitatory and inhibitory neurons interact in a CO2/H+-dependent manner to augment respiratory drive.
source: Together, these results support the possibility that the RTN functions as a CO2/H+-sensing network where excitatory and inhibitory neurons interact in a CO2/H+-dependent manner to augment respiratory drive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined synaptic recording data showing differential effects of CO2/H+ on excitatory and inhibitory inputs.

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of Sst+ parafacial neurons increased respiratory frequency (F1,5=148.1, p<0.0001).
source: Consistent with our cellular (Figure 2) and synaptic data (Figures 3–4), we found that chemogenetic suppression of Sst+ parafacial neurons increased respiratory frequency (F1,5=148.1, p<0.0001) (Figure 5A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by plethysmography data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of Sst+ parafacial neurons increased tidal volume (F1,5 = 7.360, p=0.0421).
source: tidal volume (F1,5 = 7.360, p=0.0421) (Figure 5C)
evidence: This claim is supported by plethysmography data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of Sst+ parafacial neurons increased minute ventilation (F1,5 = 81.06, p=0.0003) under baseline conditions.
source: and minute ventilation (F1,5 = 81.06, p=0.0003) under baseline conditions (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by plethysmography data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Clozapine and saline treated mice showed similar ventilatory responses to CO2 (F1,5 = 0.9089, p>0.05).
source: However, clozapine and saline treated mice showed similar ventilatory responses to CO2 (F1,5 = 0.9089, p>0.05) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by plethysmography data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of Pvalb+ parafacial neurons minimally affected baseline breathing (F1,5 = 0.0139, p>0.05).
source: Interestingly, parallel experiments performed in PvalbCre (JAX #: 008069) (F1,5 = 0.0139, p>0.05) and CckCre (JAX #: 012706) (F1,5 = 0.0660, p>0.05) minimally affected baseline breathing or the ventilatory response to CO2 (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by plethysmography data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of Cck+ parafacial neurons minimally affected baseline breathing (F1,5 = 0.0660, p>0.05).
source: Interestingly, parallel experiments performed in PvalbCre (JAX #: 008069) (F1,5 = 0.0139, p>0.05) and CckCre (JAX #: 012706) (F1,5 = 0.0660, p>0.05) minimally affected baseline breathing or the ventilatory response to CO2 (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by plethysmography data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cell type-specific expression of Cre recombinase in SstCre, PvalbCre and CckCre lines have been confirmed previously.
source: It should be noted that cell type-specific expression of Cre recombinase in SstCre (Soumier and Sibille, 2014), PvalbCre (Liu et al., 2019) and CckCre (Matsuda et al., 2020) lines have been confirmed previously.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work validating the mouse lines.

claim: Sst+ parafacial neurons are specialized to sense changes in CO2/H+ and contribute to respiratory activity.
source: Together with our cellular evidence, these results suggest Sst+ parafacial neurons are specialized to sense changes in CO2/H+ and contribute to respiratory activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined cellular, synaptic, and behavioral data.

claim: The ventral parafacial region contains Sst, Ndnf, Pvalb, and Cck classes of interneurons of which only Sst-expressing neurons are inhibited by CO2/H+.
source: Specifically, we show that (1) the ventral parafacial region contains Sst, Ndnf, Pvalb, and Cck classes of interneurons of which only Sst-expressing neurons are inhibited by CO2/H+
evidence: This is a summary of findings from scRNA-seq and electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Chemosensitive RTN neurons receive inhibitory input under control conditions that is withdrawn during exposure to high CO2.
source: (2) chemosensitive RTN neurons receive inhibitory input under control conditions that is withdrawn during exposure to high CO2
evidence: This is a summary of findings from synaptic recording experiments.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of Sst+ but not Pvalb+ or Cck+ parafacial neurons increases baseline respiratory activity.
source: (3) chemogenetic inhibition of Sst+ but not Pvalb+ or Cck+ parafacial neurons increases baseline respiratory activity.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from in vivo chemogenetic experiments.

claim: Sst-expressing parafacial neurons are important determinants of respiratory activity under baseline conditions.
source: These results suggest Sst-expressing parafacial neurons are important determinants of respiratory activity under baseline conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined experimental findings.

claim: Disruption of baseline breathing is the root cause of disordered breathing in various disease states.
source: This is important because disruption of baseline breathing is the root cause of disordered breathing in various disease states.
evidence: This is a statement of general knowledge about breathing disorders.

claim: Both Nmb+ populations likely function as chemoreceptors based on Gpr4 and Kcnk5 expression.
source: Based on Gpr4 and Kcnk5 expression both Nmb+ subtypes likely function as chemoreceptors
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns from scRNA-seq data.

claim: CO2/H+-activated Phox2b+ parafacial neurons contribute to pre-inspiratory rhythmogenesis early in development.
source: however, CO2/H+-activated Phox2b+ parafacial neurons also contribute to pre-inspiratory rhythmogenesis early in development (Onimaru et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Selective activation of ventral parafacial Phox2b-expressing neurons increased expiratory activity.
source: For example, selective activation (Souza et al., 2020) or inhibition (Marina et al., 2010) of ventral parafacial Phox2b-expressing neurons increased and decreased expiratory activity, respectively
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Selective inhibition of ventral parafacial Phox2b-expressing neurons decreased expiratory activity.
source: For example, selective activation (Souza et al., 2020) or inhibition (Marina et al., 2010) of ventral parafacial Phox2b-expressing neurons increased and decreased expiratory activity, respectively
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Expiratory parafacial neurons are not Phox2b-immunoreactive.
source: However, others have shown that expiratory parafacial neurons are not Phox2b-immunoreactive (de Britto and Moraes, 2017), suggesting these neurons are distinct from RTN chemoreceptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Expiratory parafacial neurons are putatively glutamatergic.
source: In any case, since expiratory parafacial neurons are putatively glutamatergic (Silva et al., 2016), this population is most likely included in clusters 1–3.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and inference about cluster identity.

claim: Phox2b is expressed by multiple cell types in the parafacial region.
source: Nonetheless, it is also important to recognize that Phox2b is expressed by multiple cell types in the parafacial region, thus confounding interpretation of previous work that relied primarily on Phox2b expression to target RTN chemoreceptors (Gourine et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on scRNA-seq data showing Phox2b expression in multiple clusters, with citation to prior work that may be affected by this issue.

claim: The ventral parafacial region did not include Htra3-expressing inhibitory neurons.
source: We also found the ventral parafacial region did not include Htra3-, Vip-, or Npy-expressing inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing absence of these markers.

claim: Htra3+ inhibitory neurons represent ~30% of the total interneuron population in the cortex.
source: This is in marked contrast to the cortex where Htra3+ inhibitory neurons represent ~30% of the total interneuron population (Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work about cortical interneurons.

claim: Defining the diversity of inhibitory neurons in the brainstem region provides a basis for understanding how disruption of inhibitory neural function in diseases like Dravet syndrome cause brainstem dysfunction and mortality.
source: By defining the diversity if inhibitory neurons in this brainstem region, these results provide a basis for understanding how disruption of inhibitory neural function in diseases like Dravet syndrome cause brainstem disfunction and mortality.
evidence: This is an inference about the significance of the findings for understanding disease mechanisms.

claim: Any neurons in the RTN region that respond to CO2/H+ might do so in a manner tailored to support the chemoreceptor reflex.
source: The RTN is an important respiratory chemoreceptor region (Guyenet et al., 2019); therefore, it is reasonable to speculate that any neurons in this region that respond to CO2/H+ might do so in a manner tailored to support this reflex.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known function of the RTN region.

claim: Sst+ parafacial neurons are specialized to contribute to RTN chemoreceptors and respiratory drive.
source: Since the majority of inhibitory neurons in this region did not respond to this level of CO2, it is tempting to speculate that Sst+ parafacial neurons are specialized to contribute to RTN chemoreceptors and respiratory drive.
evidence: This is speculation based on the selective CO2/H+ sensitivity of Sst+ neurons.

claim: RTN neurons including CO2/H+-activated (presumably chemoreceptors) and -inhibited (most likely Slc32a1+ based on evidence presented in this study) interact through paucisynaptic connections.
source: Previous evidence based on multi-electrode extracellular recordings from cats suggests that RTN neurons including CO2/H+-activated (presumably chemoreceptors) and -inhibited (most likely Slc32a1+ based on evidence presented in this study) interact through paucisynaptic connections (Ott et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work, with inference about cell type identity based on current findings.

claim: Mechanisms contributing to CO2/H+-induced activation of the RTN network likely involves both pre- and post-synaptic mechanisms.
source: Mechanisms contributing to CO2/H+-induced activation of the RTN network likely involves both pre- and post-synaptic mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the synaptic recording data.

claim: Other chemosensitive RTN neurons or medullary raphe neurons which may co-release glutamate are the most likely sources of CO2/H+ dependent glutamatergic drive to RTN chemoreceptors.
source: At the presynaptic level, we consider other chemosensitive RTN neurons or medullary raphe neurons which may co-release glutamate (El Mestikawy et al., 2011) as most the likely sources of CO2/H+ dependent glutamatergic drive to RTN chemoreceptors.
evidence: This is speculation about the source of excitatory input, with citation to prior work about glutamate co-release.

claim: CO2/H+-inhibited parafacial Slc32a1+ neurons are the most likely substrate responsible for CO2/H+-induced suppression of sIPSC frequency.
source: Also, since CO2/H+ inhibited the activity of some parafacial Slc32a1+ neurons, we consider these cells the most likely substrate responsible for CO2/H+-induced suppression of sIPSC frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cellular and synaptic recording data.

claim: Few inhibitory parafacial neurons were activated by CO2/H+, suggesting RTN chemoreceptors do not project to and regulate activity of parafacial inhibitory neurons.
source: It should be noted that few inhibitory parafacial neurons were activated by CO2/H+ (Figure 3C), suggesting RTN chemoreceptors do not project to and regulate activity of parafacial inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low proportion of CO2/H+-activated inhibitory neurons.

claim: The RTN receives inhibitory input from various elements of the respiratory circuit that serves to limit chemoreceptor function during times of high respiratory activity.
source: However, the RTN (Guyenet et al., 2005; Takakura et al., 2007; Yang and Feldman, 2018) and parafacial region (Silva et al., 2020) receive inhibitory input from various elements of the respiratory circuit that serves to limit chemoreceptor function during times of high respiratory activity
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CO2/H+ may elicit release of non-glutamatergic neuromodulators that alter postsynaptic conductance and potentially contribute to diminished IPSC amplitude.
source: It should also be noted that CO2/H+ may elicit release of non-glutamatergic neuromodulators that alter postsynaptic conductance and potentially contribute to diminished IPSC amplitude; however, we consider this unlikely since this non-specific mechanism is expected to affect both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative mechanisms, which is then argued against based on the differential effects observed.

claim: CO2/H+-inhibited cells have been found in several putative chemosensitive regions.
source: For example, CO2/H+-inhibited cells have been found in several putative chemosensitive regions (Conrad et al., 2009; Nichols et al., 2009; Wang and Richerson, 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GABAergic neurons in the medullary raphe are CO2/H+-inhibited.
source: including GABAergic neurons in the medullary raphe (Iceman et al., 2014) and parafacial region (Kuribayashi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GABAergic neurons in the parafacial region are CO2/H+-inhibited.
source: including GABAergic neurons in the medullary raphe (Iceman et al., 2014) and parafacial region (Kuribayashi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Application of bicuculline (GABAA receptor blocker) to the ventrolateral medulla increased inspiratory activity under control conditions but not during exposure to high CO2 in anesthetized rats.
source: These results are consistent with pharmacological evidence from anesthetized rats showing that application of bicuculline (GABAA receptor blocker) to the ventrolateral medulla increased inspiratory activity under control conditions but not during exposure to high CO2 (Gourine and Spyer, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Disinhibition of neurons located more laterally in the ventral parafacial region contributed to emergence of active expiration during exposure to high CO2.
source: Furthermore, disinhibition of neurons located more laterally in the ventral parafacial region contributed to emergence of active expiration during exposure to high CO2 (Huckstepp et al., 2015; Pagliardini et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GABAergic neurons in medullary raphe regions regulate expiratory output of the lateral parafacial region during high CO2.
source: Recent work suggests GABAergic neurons in medullary raphe regions regulate expiratory output of the lateral parafacial region during high CO2 (60)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (reference number 60 in the text).

claim: Sst+ parafacial neurons are ideal candidates for regulating expiratory activity based on their CO2/H+ response and proximity to the lateral parafacial region.
source: Our evidence that Sst+ parafacial neurons show a CO2/H+ response consistent with disinhibition and their close proximity to the lateral parafacial region makes them ideal candidates for such a function.
evidence: This is speculation based on the properties of Sst+ neurons and their anatomical location.

claim: The ability of respiratory chemoreceptors to sense and respond to tissue CO2/H+ is what maintains breathing during sleep.
source: The ability of respiratory chemoreceptors to sense and respond to tissue CO2/H+ is what maintains breathing during sleep.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about respiratory control during sleep.

claim: Baseline CO2 levels and the apneic threshold are critical determinants of stable breathing during sleep.
source: Therefore, baseline CO2 levels and the apneic threshold are critical determinants of stable breathing during sleep (Nakayama et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Ventral parafacial Sst+ neurons are important determinants of baseline CO2 levels and the apneic threshold.
source: The ability of ventral parafacial Sst+ neurons to respond to CO2 in the low physiological range (minimally active under high CO2 conditions) and preferentially regulate baseline breathing suggests these cells are important determinants of baseline CO2 levels and the apneic threshold.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CO2/H+ response profile and functional effects of Sst+ neurons.

claim: A yet unidentified population of Slc32a1+ neurons in nearby and potentially overlapping medullary regions regulate rapid eye movement (REM) sleep.
source: Interestingly, a yet unidentified population of Slc32a1+ neurons in nearby and potentially overlapping medullary regions are known to regulate rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, where activation of these cells promotes a REM-like state and inhibition of these cells does the opposite (Weber et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CO2/H+ stimulates arousal.
source: Considering that CO2/H+ also stimulates arousal (Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CO2/H+ inhibition of parafacial Slc32a1+ neurons may suppress REM and promote arousal, thus directly coordinating chemoreceptor activity with sleep-wake state.
source: it is possible CO2/H+ inhibition of parafacial Slc32a1+ neurons suppresses REM and promotes arousal, thus directly coordinating chemoreceptor activity with sleep-wake state.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms linking CO2/H+ sensing to sleep-wake regulation.

claim: In addition to RTN chemoreceptors, Sst+ parafacial neurons likely regulate respiratory activity at other levels of the respiratory circuit.
source: An additional caveat to note is that in addition to RTN chemoreceptors, Sst+ parafacial neurons likely regulate respiratory activity at other levels of the respiratory circuit.
evidence: This is speculation about additional projection targets of Sst+ neurons.

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of all parafacial inhibitory neurons in Slc32a1Cre mice increased baseline respiratory frequency (F1,9=5.560, p=0.043).
source: We found that chemogenetic suppression of all parafacial inhibitory neurons mirrored the effects of targeted inhibition of just Sst+ neurons. For example, Slc32a1Cre mice responded to clozapine (1 mg/kg) with an increase in baseline respiratory frequency (F1,9=5.560, p=0.043)
evidence: This claim is supported by plethysmography data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of all parafacial inhibitory neurons in Slc32a1Cre mice increased tidal volume (F1,9 = 19.13, p=0.002).
source: and tidal volume (F1,9 = 19.13, p=0.002), which culminated in an increase minute ventilation (F1,9=6.017, p=0.037) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by plethysmography data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of all parafacial inhibitory neurons in Slc32a1Cre mice increased minute ventilation (F1,9=6.017, p=0.037).
source: and tidal volume (F1,9 = 19.13, p=0.002), which culminated in an increase minute ventilation (F1,9=6.017, p=0.037) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by plethysmography data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibition of all parafacial inhibitory neurons by clozapine administration in Slc32a1Cre mice minimally affected the CO2 chemoreflex (F1,9=0.0724, p>0.05).
source: Also, as observed in SstCre mice, we found that inhibition of all parafacial inhibitory neurons by clozapine administration (I.P.) in Slc32a1Cre mice minimally effected the CO2 chemoreflex (F1,9=0.0724, p>0.05) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by plethysmography data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cre recombinase is specific to inhibitory parafacial neurons in Slc32a1Cre mice (95% of TdT fluorescence co-localized with Gad67-immunoreactivity).
source: We confirmed Cre recombinase is specific to inhibitory parafacial neurons in Slc32a1Cre mice (95% of TdT fluorescence co-localized with Gad67-immunoreactivity), which confirms previously reported data (Lowery-Gionta et al., 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: Clozapine had minimal effect on respiratory activity in Slc32a1Cre mice that did not receive intracranial viral injections (F1,5=0.2399, p>0.05).
source: It should also be noted that clozapine had minimal effect on respiratory activity in Slc32a1Cre mice that did not receive intracranial viral injections (F1,5=0.2399, p>0.05) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by control plethysmography data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.
